documents.title: A meta-analysis of the association between adolescent social media use and depressive symptoms.
documents.why_tier: pools multiple studies and reports a combined estimate
institutions: Department of Psychology, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR, USA.
Department of Psychology, University of Oregon, Eugene, OR, USA. Electronic address: nallen3@uoregon.edu.
documents.quote: We found a small but significant positive correlation (k=12 studies, r=.11, p<.01) between adolescent social media use and depressive symptoms.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Shows a positive association between use and depressive symptoms.

documents.title: Adolescent social media use and mental health from adolescent and parent perspectives
documents.quote: anxiety and depressive symptoms were highest among adolescents with a relatively high number of parent-reported social media accounts and relatively high FoMO.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Higher social media use linked to higher anxiety and depression.

documents.title: Adolescent social media use and well-being
documents.quote: Results show friendship contingent self-esteem to be significantly related to social media investment, and increased stress to significantly influence well-being change.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Links social media use to increased stress affecting well‑being.

documents.title: Longitudinal Associations Between Adolescent Social Media Use and Depressive Symptoms: The Roles of Appearance-Related Social Media Consciousness and Gender
documents.quote: it did not mediate or moderate the link between time on social media and depressive symptoms in the full sample.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Finds no overall effect of time spent on depressive symptoms.

documents.title: The representation of adolescent social media use: a systematic review and content analysis of UK newspaper articles.
documents.why_tier: summarises a field rather than adding a measurement
institutions: Manchester Institute of Education, School of Environment, Education and Development, University of Manchester, Manchester, UK. jade.davies@manchester.ac.uk.
Manchester Institute of Education, School of Environment, Education and Development, University of Manchester, Manchester, UK.
documents.quote: Most headlines (58%) were negatively framed, with tabloids generally adopting a more negative tone than broadsheets.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Analyzes media representation, not actual mental health outcomes.

documents.title: Neuroscientific approaches to adolescent social media use: a review of neural correlates and potential associations to social media behaviors.
documents.why_tier: summarises a field rather than adding a measurement
institutions: Department of Neuroscience, Eastern Michigan University, Ypsilanti, Michigan, United States.
documents.quote: Adolescents' social lives are evolving rapidly, existing largely online. There are mixed findings on the effect of social media on adolescent mental health.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Provides background without reporting a specific effect.

documents.title: Social media are many things: Addressing the components and patterns of adolescent social media use.
documents.venue: Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences
documents.why_tier: summarises a field rather than adding a measurement
institutions: Department of Psychology and Neuroscience, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA.
Winston National Center on Technology Use, Brain, and Psychological Development, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, USA.
documents.quote: We advocate for more work taking this nuanced approach and for the development of a comprehensive taxonomic framework that categorizes specific online experiences afforded by social media features and content.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: No empirical result on mental health outcomes.

documents.title: The Effect of Moral Disengagement and Online Disinhibition Effect on Cyberbullying in Adolescent Social Media Users
documents.venue: International Journal of Progressive Sciences and Technologies (Medical University Varna)
documents.quote: The results showed that there was a positive effect of moral disengagement on cyberbullying behavior in adolescent social media users with an effective contribution of 23.4%.
documents.verification_scope: Quotation verified, not independent validation of the interpretation.
documents.why: Focuses on cyberbullying, not mental health.
